title: SafeDec: Constrained Decoding for Safe Autoregressive Robot Navigation Policies
one_liner: A runtime safety filter for robot policies that enforces formal behavioral guarantees without retraining the model.
lead: Modern robot navigation policies are neural networks trained on lots of real and simulated robot trajectories. They work well in practice but have a fundamental gap: they have no explicit way to guarantee that the actions they choose are safe. SafeDec plugs this gap by adding a safety filter at the moment the policy decides on an action, using formal rules written in plain symbolic language to block or redirect unsafe moves—all without retraining anything.

problem.h2: The robot policy's safety blind spot
paras: A modern robot navigation policy is a neural network that learns from thousands of recorded robot trajectories. It takes in camera images and sensor readings and outputs a sequence of motor commands (move forward, turn left, grasp object). In the lab and in real deployments, these policies generalize remarkably well—they can navigate new rooms and handle situations they never saw during training.

But there is a hidden cost. The policy is purely data-driven. It has no explicit internal representation of what counts as safe. It simply learns patterns from the data. If the data contained an unsafe move in some edge case (or if the new situation is different enough from training), nothing stops the policy from outputting that unsafe action. A robot might move toward a cliff because the training data never showed that specific cliff angle, or it might activate a gripper in an unsafe configuration because it learned a correlation that does not hold generally.

A beginner might try to collect more and more data, hoping to cover every edge case. This fails because the state space is infinite—you can never record every scenario. Or one might try to add safety constraints during training, but that requires retraining the entire policy every time a new safety rule is needed. This is slow and expensive.

callout.html: SafeDec adds a runtime safety filter that accepts or rejects each action the policy proposes, using formal logical rules to guarantee correctness without any retraining.

steps.text: Neural network generates the next action given current observation
Check whether that action, if executed, will keep the system inside the safe set
Use the formal rules (written as logical formulas) to filter down to allowed actions
Reassign probability weight to the allowed actions, preserving the policy's preference ranking among them
Robot runs the top-ranked allowed action and moves to the next state

paras: SafeDec modifies the output of the policy at decoding time. Instead of letting the neural network freely choose an action from all possibilities, SafeDec inserts a filter that masks out dangerous actions and redistributes probability mass only to the safe subset. This happens once per step and requires no training.
object.object: which actions the policy is allowed to pick from

hidden.name: whether the action keeps the system safe
paras: SafeDec needs a way to know which actions will result in a safe state. It does this by checking each candidate action against a formal specification—a set of logical rules about what states and transitions are allowed. The specification is written in Signal Temporal Logic (STL), a formal language that uses predicates (like 'distance to obstacle < 0.5 meters') and logical operators (and, or, always, eventually) to express safety rules without any ambiguity.

At runtime, for each action the policy proposes, SafeDec evaluates: if the robot takes this action from the current state, does the resulting new state satisfy all the safety rules? If yes, the action is allowed. If no, it is filtered out. This is a boolean quantity—safe or unsafe—but the paper extends it to soft penalties that reflect how close the system is to violating a rule, allowing a numerical search to pick the best allowed action.

heat.caption: Darker means this action keeps the robot safe; lighter means violates a formal rule

reads.html: A safety rule might say: if a door is in front of the robot, the door must be open before any move forward is allowed. SafeDec checks this rule for each action.

Signal Temporal Logic is a language for specifying constraints on system trajectories. An STL formula can express conditions like always distance > minimum_safe_distance, which must hold at every timestep, or eventually goal_reached within 100 steps, which must happen by a deadline.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the decoding-time filter
paras: The central idea is that safety can be checked at the moment an action is about to be executed, without waiting for the model to be retrained. Here is how it works:

First, the policy outputs a probability distribution over actions (some actions scored high, others low). Second, SafeDec maintains a formal safety specification as a set of logical constraints. Third, for each action the policy wants to consider, SafeDec simulates what the new state would be if that action runs. Fourth, SafeDec checks whether the new state violates any constraint. Fifth, any action that violates a constraint is blocked. Sixth, the remaining probability mass is redistributed among the allowed actions in a way that respects the policy's original ranking—the highest-scored allowed action becomes the new first choice. This means SafeDec is fully agnostic to the policy's internals: it does not need to know how the neural network works, only what actions it proposes.

This works because formal verification is a one-time computation per step. The specification (the safety rules) is written once by a human expert or extracted from requirements. Once written, it applies to any policy that uses the same robot and environment. A new policy can be swapped in and SafeDec still works—no retraining needed.

stages.s: Policy proposes actions and their scores
For each action, simulate its effect on the robot state
Check simulated state against the formal safety rules (STL constraints)
Filter: keep only actions whose resulting state passes all checks
Renormalize: reassign probabilities within the allowed set
Constrained distribution: highest score is now a safe action

math.words: For each candidate action, compute the cost: how much does this action violate the safety specification? If the cost is zero or negative (safe), allow it. If positive (unsafe), penalize it.
math.equation: cost(a) = max_constraint c in STL { violation_margin(c, s_next(a)) }
symbols: a candidate action the policy proposed
the next robot state if action a is executed
one of the formal safety constraints
how far the state s is from satisfying constraint c; negative means satisfied
the worst-case constraint; if any constraint fails, the action fails

worked.title: A tiny worked example: one action with two constraints
lines: Constraint 1: distance_to_wall >= 0.5 meters. Current state has wall at 0.7m. If we move forward 0.3m, wall is at 0.4m (inside the safe zone).
Constraint 2: gripper_force <= 10 Newtons. Current force is 8N. Action maintains it.
cost(a) = max(-0.1, -2) = -0.1. Action violates the distance rule, so cost is positive-ish. This action is filtered out.

math.note: The cost rolls up all constraints into one number: zero or below means safe, above means unsafe. SafeDec uses this number to decide which actions to allow, because actions with zero or negative cost satisfy all the formal safety rules, while positive cost means at least one rule is violated.

bars.h2: Filtering unsafe actions improves real-world outcomes

charts.title: Without SafeDec (naive policy)
charts.note: Policy works often but makes occasional unsafe moves; distance to walls and other obstacles shrinks dangerously.

charts.title: With SafeDec constrained decoding
charts.note: Success barely drops (policy still makes good choices), but safety violations plummet and the robot stays farther from obstacles on average.

items.b: The formal specification is wrong or incomplete.
items.html: If the STL rules do not actually describe what is safe, then SafeDec will either filter out good actions (because it mistakenly blocks them) or allow bad ones (because it mistakenly permits them), since the decoding filter can only enforce the rules it is given. The responsibility for writing correct specifications lies with the system designer. SafeDec enforces what you ask it to enforce.

items.b: The model of robot dynamics is inaccurate.
items.html: SafeDec predicts the next state by running the assumed dynamics model forward. If the real robot does not behave as the model predicts (e.g., slipping, latency, sensor noise), then the filtered action might still lead to an unsafe state. This is especially risky in high-speed or high-consequence scenarios.

items.b: Filtering too aggressively removes all allowed actions.
items.html: If the constraints are too strict or the current state is already unsafe, SafeDec may have no legal actions to choose from. In that case, the system must have a fallback behavior (usually stop or go to a safe state), but the robot may fail its task.

When the formal rules are accurate, the dynamics model is validated, and the constraints are tuned to be strict enough for safety but loose enough to allow useful behaviors, SafeDec provably prevents the robot from entering an explicitly forbidden state, because the decoding filter systematically rejects every action that would lead to a state violating any rule.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A convincing demo would take a trained navigation policy, write a simple STL rule (e.g., keep distance to obstacles above 0.5 meters), run the policy on a procedurally generated test environment with and without SafeDec, and measure: (1) how many times the robot violates the distance rule with SafeDec on versus off, and (2) how much the success rate drops due to over-aggressive filtering. A good demo would show that SafeDec catches most violations with minimal performance loss.
demo.metric_eq: safety_gain = (violations_without_filter - violations_with_filter) / violations_without_filter; performance_cost = (success_without_filter - success_with_filter) / success_without_filter
demo.closing: The demo must make it impossible to miss that SafeDec can turn an unsafe-but-successful policy into a safe-and-still-mostly-successful policy, all at runtime, without touching the model.
